issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration of rights together with an injunction is not a suit for a declaration simpliciter merely because the claimed injunction is consequential on the declaration.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration of their rights to participate in the endowment’s income and ceremonies and an injunction restraining interference with those rights.
The endowment was managed by trustees, and the claimants sought relief against persons said to obstruct their exercise of the claimed rights.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable because it sought an injunction as further relief and was not a suit for a declaration simpliciter.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act does not require dismissal of a suit seeking a declaration and an injunction; an injunction is further relief. The Court relied on Kunj Behari Prasadji Purshottam Prasadji v. Keshavlal Hiralal, which held that such a suit may be maintainable, while adequacy of the further relief depends on the circumstances of the case.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of a right.
predicates.consequential_injunction_sought: The claimant also sought an injunction to prevent interference with the exercise of that right.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks both a declaration of a right and an injunction against interference with it, the suit is maintainable as a suit for further relief rather than as a suit for a declaration alone.

issues.legal_issue: The limitation period for a suit seeking a declaration and injunction does not begin merely because a contesting defendant denies the claimed right, where the relevant trustees have neither infringed nor clearly threatened to infringe it.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration of their rights and an injunction against interference.
The suit was brought more than twelve years after the death of the person through whom the claimants asserted their rights.
The record did not show that the trustees responsible for distributing the income had denied or threatened to deny the claimants’ rights; the denial was by contesting defendants.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation merely because the contesting defendants did not recognise the claimed rights; the right to sue had not accrued without infringement or a clear and unequivocal threat by the relevant trustees.
issues.legal_principle: Article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, required the six-year period to be computed from when the right to sue accrued. A right to sue does not accrue until the asserted right is infringed or there is at least a clear and unequivocal threat to infringe it. Mere denial by a person who does not control or administer the right does not start limitation. The Court also noted that sections 6 and 8 saved the first claimant’s claim during minority, but its conclusion on limitation did not depend only on that ground.

predicates.declaratory_injunction_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking a declaration of a right and an injunction against interference with it.
predicates.relevant_trustees_control_the_claimed_ri: Trustees are responsible for administering or distributing the benefit asserted in the suit.
predicates.relevant_trustees_infringed_or_clearly_t: The trustees responsible for the benefit denied, obstructed, or clearly threatened to obstruct the claimant’s exercise of the right.

issues.definition: In a suit for a declaration and injunction concerning a right administered by trustees, a contesting defendant’s denial alone does not bar the suit for limitation purposes if the trustees have not infringed or clearly threatened the right.

issues.legal_issue: The Muslim Personal Law governs a specified personal-law issue between Muslims despite contrary custom when the proceeding was still pending, including on appeal, when the applicable law took effect.
material_facts: The parties were Muslims and disputed the distribution of income from a religious endowment, including the rights of heirs to that income.
A family custom excluded females from receiving a share of the income.
The suit remained pending on appeal when the Madras amendment to the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act took effect.
The amendment included trusts, trust properties and wakfs among the matters governed by Muslim Personal Law, notwithstanding contrary custom or usage.
issues.conclusion: The amended Act applied to the pending suit, including at the appeal stage, and the High Court was required to decide the relevant issue under Muslim Personal Law rather than the contrary custom.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, as amended by the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application (Madras Amendment) Act, 1949, made Muslim Personal Law the rule of decision for the specified matters, including trusts, trust properties and wakfs, notwithstanding contrary custom or usage. Although legislation affecting vested rights is generally presumed not to be retrospective, the breadth of the statutory direction rebutted that presumption for pending proceedings, including appeals; finally decided proceedings were unaffected. The Court disapproved Syed Roshan Ali v. Mt. Rehmat Bibi for relying on the general presumption without giving effect to the statutory language.

predicates.muslim_parties: The parties to the dispute are Muslims.
predicates.specified_personal_law_issue: The dispute concerns a matter for which the applicable law directs that Muslim Personal Law be the rule of decision.
predicates.pending_proceeding_when_law_took_effect: The suit or proceeding, including any appeal, had not been finally decided when the applicable law took effect.

issues.definition: When Muslims dispute a matter governed by the applicable personal-law rule and the proceeding remains pending when that rule takes effect, the issue is decided under that personal law despite contrary custom.

issues.legal_issue: Muslim female heirs claiming through a deceased member of a family sharing endowment income are entitled to receive their share under Muslim Personal Law, notwithstanding a custom excluding females.
material_facts: The endowment’s surplus income had long been shared among descendants in four families.
The deceased descendant had received a share of that income and was survived by his wife and daughters, who claimed through him.
The asserted family custom excluded females and persons claiming through females from receiving income.
The claimants’ entitlement concerned receipt of income; the record did not show that this entitlement was conditional on personally performing particular religious offices.
issues.conclusion: The female heirs claiming through the deceased were entitled under Muslim Personal Law to receive the income to which he was entitled; the contrary custom did not defeat their claim.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, as amended by the 1949 Madras Act, Muslim Personal Law governed the relevant succession and endowment-related questions notwithstanding contrary custom. The Court held that the claimants, as heirs claiming through the deceased, were entitled to the income under that law and observed that nothing in the record made receipt of income conditional on performing the offices of Peshimam, Khatib or Mujavar.

predicates.muslim_parties: The parties to the dispute are Muslims.

predicates.income_shared_among_family_descendants: The endowment income has been distributed among descendants of the family.

issues.definition: When women claim as heirs through a deceased income recipient in a Muslim family dispute over income shared among descendants, a custom excluding female heirs does not defeat their entitlement under personal law.

issues.legal_issue: A new appellate argument about the performance of religious offices may be declined when it was not raised before the lower appellate court, and the right to receive family income is not defeated without a basis showing that receipt depends on performing those offices.
material_facts: The defendants argued in the Supreme Court that women could not perform certain religious offices, even through deputies.
That argument had not been raised before the High Court.
The trial court had found that the duties of the offices could be performed through deputies.
Nothing in the record suggested that the right to receive income depended on performing those duties.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the defendants to raise the argument at that stage and, in any event, found no basis for treating performance of the offices as a condition of the claimants’ right to receive income.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered it unjustified to allow an argument in the appeal that had not been raised before the High Court. It also relied on the trial court’s finding that the duties could be performed through deputies and on the absence of evidence that income entitlement was conditional on performing those duties.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal in which a party advances an argument about eligibility to perform religious offices.
predicates.argument_not_raised_before_lower_appella: The party did not raise that argument before the lower appellate court.
predicates.no_record_basis_that_income_entitlement_: The record contains no basis for finding that the right to receive income depends on personally performing the religious offices.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a court may decline an argument about eligibility to perform religious offices when it was not raised below and the record does not make office performance a condition of income entitlement.
